claims.text: An actively refined neural-network interatomic potential can substantially reduce the cost of computing fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed method can preserve the fidelity of vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
Pure Al and Cu–Zn have sufficiently well-characterized solid phases for the proposed initial benchmarks.
The potential will be trained on a sparse, informative set of ab initio free-energy evaluations covering both solid and liquid configurations.
Active learning can identify high-uncertainty regions that require additional sampling.
Targeting high-uncertainty regions will reduce the number of costly explicit AIMD runs.
NPT simulations within roughly 50 K of the melting point can accurately capture the relevant phase free-energy differences.
Approximately 100 ps of molecular-dynamics sampling per phase is sufficient for the proposed high-temperature evaluation.
The neural-network potential will guide molecular-dynamics sampling of atomic configurations in both solid and liquid phases.
A trained neural-network potential can rapidly interpolate the high-dimensional free-energy landscape in place of full AIMD.
Targeted retraining allows the potential to capture vibrational and anharmonic effects.
Active learning can minimize errors specifically in configurations that most affect solid–liquid phase free energies.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD.
Phase free energies and melting temperatures from the proposed workflow will deviate by only a few percent from AIMD and TOR-TILD results.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD accurately capture the free energies of solid and liquid phases.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD are computationally expensive, particularly for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
A method initially applied to elemental and binary alloys may be extended to high-entropy systems containing up to five elements.
The proposed applicability window is approximately 0.9–1.1 times the experimental melting temperature.
